messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Product Manager
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 55

He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who comes to therapy with a careful, contained manner, as if he has spent decades making sure nothing inside him shows too much. He is married and works as a product manager, a role that has suited him for years because it lets him stay organized, solve problems, and keep his focus on practical details. In session, he speaks clearly and precisely, often returning to work, schedules, and responsibilities when the conversation moves toward anything more personal. Over time, it becomes clear that this way of speaking is not just temperament; it is a form of survival.

He does not begin with the worst parts of what happened. He starts in fragments, with the years before. He describes a period of political instability in his younger adulthood, when he becomes caught in a conflict that is not his own but quickly becomes his reality. He is taken into custody and held without certainty about how long he will remain there. The first days are confusing, then quickly become defined by pain, fear, and the loss of ordinary time. He remembers the smell of damp concrete, the sound of doors opening in the corridor, the way he tries to judge danger by footsteps before anyone enters. He says that after a while, he stops hoping each time he is taken somewhere, because hope itself becomes exhausting.

What he describes as torture is not told in a single dramatic sequence but in repeated scenes that return to him with the force of present tense. He is beaten, threatened, deprived of sleep, and left in positions that make his body shake and cramp. The humiliation is as lasting as the pain. He recalls being spoken to like an object, and he carries the memory of not knowing whether the next hour will bring more questions, more punishment, or silence. He learns to keep his face neutral, to answer cautiously, to disappear inward. Even now, decades later, he says there is a part of him that still feels it must monitor every room, every tone of voice, every pause.

When he is eventually released, he expects relief. Instead, he finds that leaving does not mean returning to who he was. In the early years after the trauma, he lives with a body that startles at sudden sounds and a mind that seems to move without permission back into the cell. He does not like being touched unexpectedly, even by people he loves. Loud voices make his chest tighten. He becomes watchful in crowds and prefers to sit where he can see exits. He develops a habit of scanning faces for anger before it is spoken. Sleep is difficult; when he does drift off, he wakes tense and alert, often from dreams he cannot fully describe, only the sensation of dread that lingers after them.

He marries and builds a life, and in many ways he functions well. At work, he becomes known as dependable, composed, and meticulous. As a product manager, he is good at anticipating problems and managing competing demands, and colleagues likely experience him as steady. Yet the same vigilance that makes him effective also keeps him braced. He overprepares, checks and rechecks his work, and feels a sharp unease when plans change without warning. He is often exhausted by the effort of appearing calm. He says that he can lead meetings and make decisions all day, then come home and feel emptied out, unable to explain why he is so tired.

In his marriage, he is loving but guarded. His wife knows some of the story, though not all of it, because he has spent years protecting her from details he fears would burden her. He shows care through responsibility rather than words, through making sure the home is secure, the bills are paid, the family is cared for. At the same time, intimacy can make him feel exposed. When he is upset, he tends to withdraw rather than speak. He is ashamed of how quickly his body reacts to reminders, ashamed that even now, after building a successful life, part of him still expects cruelty.

As he grows older, the memories do not soften in the way he once hoped they would. Instead, they have become more organized and more available, arriving with a force that surprises him. Certain news stories, confinement, or even medical procedures can pull him back into the past. He notices that his patience is thinner than it used to be, and that he can become irritable when he feels trapped or questioned. Still, he keeps going. He works, he maintains his routines, and he comes to sessions because he wants, in his words, “to stop living as if it is happening again.” He sits with that wish carefully, as though it is both fragile and necessary, while the memory of what was done to him continues to shape the way he moves through the world.
